messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 26
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: Latin American
  relationship_status: Single
  occupation: School Counselor
  trauma_type: Witnessed domestic violence (childhood)
  pcl5: 40

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Maladaptive Strategies: Hypervigilance towards people: vigilant for dangerous people, Avoid Location: Going to or near the place where the event happened, Rumination: Prevention: ruminate about how event could have been prevented
  Threat: Alert at Home: I feel on guard even inside my own home, Back to Wall: I feel unsafe unless my back is against a wall where I can see the room, Startle to Touch: I react with alarm when someone touches me unexpectedly
  Memory: Cannot Explain Clearly: When I try to explain what happened I lose the thread and cannot finish, Overwhelm on Recall: When the memory returns I feel so overwhelmed by emotion that I have to stop, Triggered Without Warning: Something in my surroundings can instantly bring back the full memory without warning
  Negative Appraisals: Institutional Failure: The people or institutions that should have protected me let me down, Mistrust: People can't be trusted, Self-Blame: The event happened because of the way I acted

Active components (must all appear in the vignette, even if not causally connected):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals

Required causal connections — the vignette must convey each of these within a paragraph:
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Marisol Ortega is a 26-year-old school counselor who grew up in a small apartment where, as a child, she repeatedly witnessed her mother being assaulted by her stepfather. In one memory she returns to often, she is standing in the hallway outside the kitchen, hearing a chair scrape hard across the floor and her mother’s voice change from arguing to pleading. She remembers freezing near the wall, trying to make herself invisible while still watching the doorway, convinced that if she had said something sooner, called someone, or not hesitated, she might have stopped what happened. What stays with her just as strongly is that neighbors heard and did nothing, and that adults who knew there was trouble never protected them. Over time she had come to believe both that the people who were supposed to keep children safe had failed her and that safety depended on her own constant readiness, because people could not be trusted.

Those beliefs shaped the way the memories settled in her. When Marisol tries to describe the violence directly, she often loses the thread, stalls, and says she “can’t get it out in order.” If she pushes herself to keep going, she becomes flooded quickly and has to stop. The memory does not feel like a finished story from childhood but something that can arrive whole and suddenly. A man’s raised voice in a school hallway, the slam of a classroom door, or the scrape of metal chair legs on tile can bring back the kitchen and hallway without warning. In those moments, what comes with the image is not only fear but the old conclusion that adults did not step in and that she herself failed to do the right thing.

Now, even in her own apartment, Marisol feels on guard. She checks where exits are when she enters a room and sits with her back against a wall whenever she can, including in staff meetings at school, where she chooses the chair in the corner that lets her see the door and everyone’s hands. If a colleague brushes past her unexpectedly, she startles sharply and her body reacts before she can orient herself. She is certain that danger comes from people, especially from shifts in tone, posture, or movement that others seem to ignore. Because she mistrusts people so deeply, vigilance feels necessary rather than excessive; to her, letting down her guard would mean repeating the mistake of assuming someone else will keep things safe.

That sense of threat has narrowed her life over the past few years. Marisol avoids the neighborhood where she grew up and will take a longer route across town rather than pass the block where the apartment still stands. At work, when parents begin arguing in the counseling office or a father’s voice grows forceful, she finds reasons to step out or call someone else in, while telling herself she is being practical. At home she goes over and over the old scenes, ruminating on what could have prevented the violence—if she had run to a neighbor sooner, if she had spoken differently, if some adult had been pushed harder to act. The more she scans people for danger and arranges herself to stay protected, the more alert she feels, and the more convinced she becomes that mistrust is simply realism.

Her memories also drive these habits directly. Because reminders can pull the whole scene back without warning and overwhelm her so fast, she tries to stay ahead of them by controlling where she goes and who is around her. Avoiding that part of the city makes sense to her because she fears being hit by the memory in the middle of the day. Watching people closely at school feels like preparation against the next sudden jolt. Yet this constant readiness seems to keep the memory close to the surface; the scrape of chairs in the cafeteria, a student flinching at a loud male voice, or an unexpected touch in a crowded hallway can set her off again, and afterward she is left shaken, more watchful, and more certain that the world is unsafe.

As these episodes repeat, her interpretations harden further. When she is startled or overwhelmed, she takes it as proof that she has never really been safe and that others still cannot be relied upon to notice harm until it is too late. She also reads her own distress as evidence that she failed somehow at the time, that there was a right action she did not take. Recently, after freezing during a tense meeting with separated parents at school and needing to leave abruptly when the father stood and raised his voice, she felt humiliated and frightened by how instantly she was back in the apartment hallway. That incident, along with the strain of feeling guarded even in her own home, is what brought her to treatment. What frightens Marisol most is the idea that she will always live as if violence is about to enter the room; what she hopes for, cautiously, is to be able to sit through a conversation, come home, and not feel she has to keep watch every minute.
